gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/10343.text: A comic essay that pretends to retell a Chinese manuscript: a boy named Bo-bo burns down his father's cottage and, with it, a litter of pigs, and discovers roast pork by accident. Lamb enjoys the mock-learned tone, and the essay turns into an extended appreciation of crackling and of eating. It is one of the best known of his Elia essays.

gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2048/.text: Irving visits an English village church and finds in it a small theatre of rank: ancient tombs, and a congregation of the neighbouring gentry in cushioned, gilded pews. He observes the Sunday gathering with affection and some irony, and the essay shows how his Sketch Book looked at English country life as an outsider. It is a short, gentle piece with plenty to notice.

gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/26659.text: James argues that no ethical philosophy can be completed in advance, because everyone who lives a moral life adds something to what ethics is. He rejects both the sceptic and the dogmatist and asks what a thinker looking for a system of moral relations should expect from the world. Written as a lecture, it is demanding but clear, and typical of how James wrote about philosophy for general readers.

gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/70/pg.text: Mark Twain reports from Bayreuth in 1891, where crowds of devotees travel from across the world to hear Wagner's operas, as in a pilgrimage. The opening is a comic account of packed trains, scarce seats and lodgings, and a town transformed by one composer. It is among the funniest pieces in What Is Man? and Other Essays, and it works as a portrait of devotion as much as of music.

gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/79560.text: Goldsmith argues that verse is a pattern of long and short syllables that goes back to the measured music of the first songs and hymns. He is impatient with critics who set rhyme against the ancient feet as if they were opposites, and he points out that the word rhyme comes from a Greek word for number. It is a short, opinionated essay on a technical subject, written for readers who are not schoolmasters.

gutenberg:gutenberg.org/cache/epub/9846/.text: Thoreau and a friend set out on foot from Concord in July 1842 for Mount Wachusett, a hill they had watched on the horizon for years. The essay begins with how distance can turn ordinary hills into the mountains of poetry, then follows the walk itself. It is a friendly early piece, written when Thoreau was in his twenties.

libraryofshortstories:libraryofshortstor.text: An old fisherman takes a visitor to a cliff on the Norwegian coast and tells how he survived being drawn into a great whirlpool, which turned his hair white. Poe builds the account from precise observation: the shape of the vortex, the way different objects sink, and the fisherman's reasoning that helps him. It is one of his adventure tales, closer to physics than to the supernatural.

An old man tells the tall tale of how the American Revolution really began, according to his great-aunt: with a farmer called Lige Butterwick and his tooth, and with Paul Revere's workshop. The narration sounds like talk by the fire, with digressions and a straight face about the whole thing being true. Stephen Vincent Benet wrote it in 1937, and it plays on the way family stories compete with the history in books.

A narrator remembers a friend from the sunny south who arrived in Petersburg one winter morning full of health and plain-spoken warmth and would not take no for an answer at the door. Kuprin sets that vitality against the grey, crowded city, and the title suggests what Petersburg will do to him. Douglas Ashby's translation keeps the voice conversational, like a friend telling a story.

At a girls' school the principal has decided that every subject for the year will revolve around Napoleon, so the music pupils practise the Eroica, the needlework class designs Empire gowns and the literature class reads War and Peace. Forster follows the teachers who have to make the scheme work, with gentle mockery. It is a short comic story about enthusiasm for a system that outruns common sense.

A cheerful, self-satisfied young man takes his mother to a mountaineering inn in the Alps and goes off to show the climbers how it should be done, to their irritation. Wells tells it as a boastful first-person comedy, full of his narrator's opinions on vegetarianism, aeroplanes and the dingy gentlemen of the climbing set. The title suggests whose story it really is.

In a bush pub the shearers talk about an absent man, Macquarie, who is better known than liked, until the old drunk in the corner shouts that he is a mate of his. Henry Lawson tells the scene in the speech of the bush, and the rest of the story turns on what the old man has to say about him. At about fifteen hundred words, it shows how Lawson makes a whole bar and a life out of dialogue.

On a Sunday afternoon Miss Brill, an Englishwoman in a French town, puts on her fur and goes to the public gardens to listen to the band and watch the people. She enjoys thinking of the whole scene as a play in which everyone, herself included, has a part. Katherine Mansfield tells it in a few pages, and the last page changes what the first pages mean.

In a ship's log, a captain notes that his first and second mates have bought a hundred pounds of saccharine to smuggle past the English Customs, and are quarrelling over how to hide it. Their plan involves a sealed paint drum lowered over the side on a line. William Hope Hodgson, who spent years at sea, writes it as a dry comic tale in which the details of the scheme matter.

A Father Brown story that opens in Paris with two young followers of the famous scientist and moralist Dr Hirsch, whose causes include striking a farewell from the French classics and altering the Marseillaise. Chesterton pokes fun at their ideas before the plot, a duel, gets going. It is a detective story that is also a comedy about fashionable opinions.

Sherlock Holmes is called in by an old schoolfellow of Watson's, a young Foreign Office clerk who has lost a secret naval treaty from his office and his career with it. The case unfolds through the circumstances of one evening at the office and a few small clues that Holmes notices and others do not. It is one of the longer Holmes stories, with a good puzzle and a satisfying explanation.

Told as entries in a doctor's diary, the story begins with a young man who asks to be examined for a growth on his side: a fully formed small right hand, which has grown steadily over the last three months. The doctor tells the case in clinical, careful prose, which sets up the horror. Anthony Rud's story first appeared in Weird Tales and runs about three thousand words.

Told as a fairy tale set on a Texas cattle ranch, the story introduces a rancher's daughter, Josefa O'Donnell, who rides at a gallop and can put bullets through a tin can swinging on a string. The narrator winks at the reader throughout and promises a chronicle of the princess, a happy thought and a big cat that bungled its job. It is a short comic tale with a plot that turns on a surprise.

Mary Shelley's narrator sets out from Rome on a spring day to see the lake at Albano, and the story begins with a long, vivid look at the countryside, the fireflies and the hills. Written for the gift annual The Keepsake in 1828, it moves from travel writing into a tale of two sisters, whom the title names. The setting is Italian and the prose is leisurely.

North of the old town of Kingsport a cliff juts into the sky, and the sea mist that rises from it carries dreams of ocean and old secrets. Lovecraft opens in a lush, almost poetic voice, setting up a high, strange house that the sailors look to as they look to a star. It belongs to his dreamier, less violent mode, first printed in Weird Tales.

An artist unhappy with a portrait of an organ-grinder, which he feels is a painting and not a living thing, wishes that his imagination could make a man. Wells frames the story as an account nobody can check, resting on the painter's own word. It is a short comic fantasy about creativity, and it runs to under two thousand words.

A traveller on his way from Algiers to the Sahara stops for tea in a small village and meets an Englishman who claims to have seen Satan. Lord Dunsany sets the encounter in a landscape of Roman ruins and camels, and the title promises sworn testimony. It is a quiet, uncanny tale from his later years, first printed in a fantasy magazine in 1953.

Two Dublin friends, Corley and Lenehan, spend a summer evening walking the city while Corley talks about his latest conquest and what he hopes to get from it. Joyce writes in plain, exact prose with no comment on his characters, and the story follows them street by street until a single small gesture at the end carries all the meaning. It is one of the shorter stories in Dubliners.

Tolstoy retells a legend said to come from the Indians of South America: God first made people so that they did not need to work, found them quarrelling, and then arranged things so that they would have to work together. The story is under nine hundred words and moves like a fable, with God returning to check on his experiment. It is a compact example of how Tolstoy turned a moral question into a simple parable.

lithub:lithub.com/across-the-street.text: A fifty-eight-year-old man who has lived in group homes and institutions moves into a house of his own in a subdivision, set up by his parents, one hopeful and one worn out. The neighbours decide he is peculiar, and they watch him and talk. The story becomes a study of what neighbours see, what they decide not to see, and how a community makes room for someone it does not understand.

lithub:lithub.com/altogether-elsewhere-v.text: In a future after the Singularity, a girl whose parents asked their friends to give her a little of themselves welcomes her mother, an Ancient who lived in the flesh until twenty-six before uploading. The mother has left the family once and has things she wants to say. Ken Liu tells it through the silent thoughts people exchange, and it asks what parents owe a child when everyone can be copied.

lithub:lithub.com/animal-crackers.text: A bestiary of deadpan entries, each about a single animal, that begins like an encyclopedia and drifts into comic non sequiturs about anxiety, college, nuclear attack and Dostoyevsky. The first two entries, on the muskrat and the pangolin, will tell you whether the voice is for you. Sam Savage, the novelist who wrote Firmin, builds the jokes out of short flat sentences that get funnier as they pile up.

lithub:lithub.com/at-last-the-escalade.text: A family road trip nearly over, a father and two boys stop at a gorge to pee, and a bear steps out of the trees. The story slows down the seconds that follow, setting what the safety pamphlets say about bears against what actually happens, and moves between the boys' fear and the bear's own point of view. It is short, quick and funny until it is not.

lithub:lithub.com/cambridge-people.text: A woman walking home from dinner sees her own apartment advertised for sale in an estate agent's window, photographed so that it looks like the place she lives and not like it. Her landlords plan open houses every Saturday until it sells, so strangers will walk through her belongings. The story starts from a small humiliation and sets it against the three years she has spent there.

lithub:lithub.com/cocoon.text: The narrator works for a father's pest-control company, good at identifying infestations from the faintest clues and privately repelled by insects, while hiding a part of themselves that comes out in front of the mirror. When the father hires a new worker, Tyronne, the secrets in the household start to shift. The insect detail is precise, and the title takes its meaning from it.

lithub:lithub.com/entropy-by-arthur-sze.text: A poem that circles back on itself: each line returns later in a different position, so that images of toxic runoff from roofs, a park ranger's patter about the Anasazi, a trash truck, land mines and an axolotl trying to regrow its lungs keep recombining. The effect is of a day in which small and enormous things pass side by side. Arthur Sze, who has written twelve books of poetry, builds the poem from its own repetitions, which suits its title.

lithub:lithub.com/floor-plans.text: A married couple agree to divorce in the story's first moments, and the narrator describes the practical, polite way her husband proposes to split everything, down to the apartment they both want. She watches a neighbour's piano being hoisted through a window while she works out what she is losing. The story pays attention to small things: moles on a cheek, who gets up first, how a marriage ends quietly.

lithub:lithub.com/maheov.text: The story opens with a Cheyenne boy's name and the secrets folded into it: a twin who died at birth, a mother medically sterilised, and the Cheyenne word for God hidden inside the word for the colour orange. Tommy Orange, author of There There, writes with dark humour about Native lives in the United States. This is a story about a family's history and about how institutions treated it.

lithub:lithub.com/paradise.text: Rita is a new arrival in Arizona, looking out of the window of her English class and trying to find a poetic word for the desert that will help her learn to love it. She cannot, and she remembers that the Arabic word is more beautiful. The story, part of a collection published free by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, follows a girl between two languages and a new school where she does not yet understand the jokes.

lithub:lithub.com/psalm-under-seige.text: A very short poem that names Syrian places: Arwad, Idlib, Daraa. Fishermen come back empty-handed, fields are stripped by locusts, wells are dry, and the speaker's last proof of being alive is a candle flame. Khaled Mattawa, who also translates contemporary Arabic poetry, wrote it for his collection Fugitive Atlas.

lithub:lithub.com/savage.text: Set in London in 1820, the story is narrated by an older man whose late brother's son has just arrived after a long absence, a boy whose heritage shows only in his hair, lips and the tinge of his skin. The narrator sets strict terms for how little of his own life he will give up, and the telling is formal and reserved. The story keeps asking what he is not saying about the boy and about the family's past.

lithub:lithub.com/soldiers.text: A boy remembers a Saturday in Los Angeles when his father, out of work for months, was off drinking with two old friends, and his mother was begging for her job back at a farm stand. The narrator is about to turn twelve and is supposed to be grounded, and the day is set up with his parents' tensions all around him. Scott O'Connor writes in a plain, observant voice that lets what the boy sees do the telling.

lithub:lithub.com/stage-13.text: Yoni is thirty-four, a failed Hollywood director with nearly a hundred thousand dollars of student debt and a plan to move home to Queens and work for a mulch business. A call from a Los Angeles number interrupts his search for flights, and the story turns on what it offers him. Simon Rich is known for short comic fiction, and the first paragraph shows how funny the details will be.

lithub:lithub.com/stick-season.text: A grieving couple from Brooklyn drive their converted van to a newly renovated inn that has offered them a free stay in exchange for a write-up. On the way they listen to a podcast about a plane crash in the Andes, which gives them something to think about other than themselves. The story sets up an uneasy weekend where the half-finished inn and the bare November trees echo their mood.

lithub:lithub.com/the-echo-a-poem-by-mar.text: A poem in long, prose-like lines that moves between a snow globe, a story about an empress whose golden hair was buried in a domed tomb, a shower, and snow falling on a city. Under the images is grief: the speaker cannot make sense of how absolute death is, and keeps setting one moment aside so that the next can arrive. It comes from Mary Jo Bang's collection A Film in Which I Play Everyone and is dedicated to the poet Lucie Brock-Broido.

lithub:lithub.com/the-elephant.text: A city plagued by drought is consumed by the disappearance of its elephant, which newspapers and officials treat as a crisis of public trust. The narrator and her husband Apat live through the rumours, from a secret burial to an elephant that melted like ice cream. Audrey Heijns's translation keeps the deadpan tone, and the story is a comedy about how bureaucracy and gossip respond to an absurd event.

lithub:lithub.com/the-invisible.text: A village that speaks as a single voice, we, hears from Martha about Mr Ingram and his Invisible daughter, who live in a grand mansion across the lake and attend the Wednesday market. The villagers go and look, find only bog and gorse, and argue about whether Martha is lying or losing her wits. Jo Lloyd tells it with dry humour, and the collective voice gives it the feel of a fable about what a community decides to believe.

lithub:lithub.com/the-nightingale-that-s.text: Told in the manner of a traditional Arabic tale, the story begins with a king who orders the whole city dark for one night to test his people's loyalty. Three sisters keep spinning by a lamp hidden under a bowl pierced with holes, and the king and his vizier, disguised as dervishes, overhear what each of them wishes for. Inea Bushnaq's translation keeps the pattern of three wishes, and the title promises a bird that speaks.

lithub:lithub.com/there-he-go.text: A girl named Latonya grows up with one photograph of her grandfather, a faded figure at the edge of a picture who becomes, for her, the coolest man who ever lived. The story begins with the single line her mother says to her when she is nine, and follows how a family's half-told stories shape a child's idea of who she comes from. Ladee Hubbard writes in a voice that moves easily between wonder and wariness.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/ann.text: A widow takes her husband's urn down from a high shelf on the anniversary of their wedding, undresses as she did on their wedding night, and tips his ashes into her bath. The rhymed stanzas keep the tone brisk, even comic, while the final lines settle into something close to devotion. It turns a macabre act into a picture of a marriage that is still going on.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/col.text: Olive Senior, a Jamaican poet, remembers a girls' school that taught Latin declensions, English kings and Canadian wheatfields while saying nothing about the island outside the window. A refrain returns after each list of lessons to mark what was missing, and slowly the voice takes back the speech the school punished as bad talking. It works as a memoir of schooling and as an argument about who a curriculum is for.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/gra.text: A language teacher takes his students through the tenses, from the perfect and simple past to reported speech, and uses each grammar point to talk about a relationship. A sentence in the future simple about fine weather is clouded over as the tense changes, and the poem lets the grammar carry the sense of loss. It is written in rhyming couplets, and Stephen Romer is also a translator of French poetry.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/por.text: The speaker looks at a portrait at the foot of the bed in which someone is dying, painted when the sitter was twenty-five, and notices that the body now looks like a chalk sketch. A joke about Dorian Gray makes the dying person laugh. Ella Duffy ends on a quiet thought about how, days before death, the person came to look more like the first draft than the last. It is short and has the plainness of something noticed in a hospital room.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/pur.text: A four-line poem built on a single object: the torn wing of a puriri moth, a large New Zealand moth, so light that breath can lift it. The speaker turns that lightness into a picture of lovers resting on a breath. It is brief and quiet, and it makes the most of what the poet can hold in her hand.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/sha.text: One unpunctuated run of words, written for a collection of poems on climate justice, that asks to be shaken out of complacency. The speaker wants to move past comfortable, consumerist habits and the guilt that drops a coin in a charity can, and to reach for alternative endings. Dorothea Smartt is a poet and performer, so the poem is worth hearing in the Poetry Archive recording as well as reading.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/tal.text: A comic talking blues in Dundee Scots: a man turns on the tap and the water answers back, announcing what it is, what it is not and how well it feels. The poem plays with the call and response of the blues and with how a Scots accent looks on the page. Herbert is a Dundee poet, and the poem is dedicated to the Scottish poet Duncan Glen.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/tel.text: The speaker asks not to be told what autumn looks like in the countryside, because he has known it for years and is about to leave it. Stanza by stanza he names the cones, the cuckoo, the sheaves and the leaves, then hands it all over to whoever comes next. The last verse is the bleak one: nature does not care whose meadow it is.

poetryarchive:poetryarchive.org/poem/you.text: A poem built on one repeated request: allow. The speaker asks for room, among managed plantations and tidy suburbs, for pine martens, capercaillies, brambles and a plain ledge of flowers. Richard Price lets sound lead as much as sense, with echoing pairs such as coughers and coffers, and the poem comes from his collection Lucky Day (2005).

publicdomainreview:publicdomainreview.or.text: Rhys Griffiths introduces Count de Waldeck, a nineteenth-century artist, publisher of erotica, explorer and general enigma, whose drawings of ancient Mesoamerican ruins are beautiful and not to be trusted, with anachronistic elephants and doubtful architecture. The essay is a short portrait of one of the century's stranger figures. It is worth reading for how much of his life remains uncertain.

Jessica Riskin tells the story of automata, the machines built over centuries to mimic living things, from a defecating duck to talking busts and mechanised figures of Christ. Her argument is that the history of artificial intelligence began long before computers, with makers asking what it would take to imitate thought and life. It is a lively essay that makes a current debate feel less new.

Matthew Green describes the London coffeehouses of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, a lively scene that looks nothing like today's chains. They were places for caffeine-fuelled debate, news, business and new ideas, and Green argues that they helped shape the modern world. The essay is a good companion for anyone who enjoys reading in cafes.

Ryan Feigenbaum follows one species of algae through eighteenth-century science, from Joseph Priestley's laboratory flasks to its possible influence on Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Algae were hardly glamorous, and the essay shows how much argument about life and matter they set off. It is a short history of how a humble plant ended up at the centre of big questions.

Mary Fissell looks at a sex manual first published in seventeenth-century London that went through hundreds of editions and was still being reprinted long afterwards. The book taught readers about conception and childbirth and, as Fissell shows, also titillated them. The essay is a good way into how ordinary people learned about their bodies before modern medicine, and why a single cheap book could last so long.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/apha.text: A family visits a woman who has suddenly lost the ability to speak, while the nurses talk in blood-pressure numbers. The poem is told from the visitors' side, with their helplessness and the way they fall apart at night once they leave the ward. Its last lines let her scrambled words appear on the page, so the title, a word for lost language, is something the reader sees as well as hears.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/argu.text: Robert Herrick opens his 1648 collection Hesperides by listing everything he will sing about: flowers, village festivals, brides and bridal cakes, fairies, and the passing of time. The last couplet adds Hell and then Heaven, with a joke about hoping to get there after all. It is a short, rhymed table of contents that doubles as a self-portrait of a cheerful poet.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/astr.text: Sidney's speaker addresses Stella as his only light and asks why she uses her sweet voice and sound reasoning to argue him out of loving her. The effort is hopeless, since her virtue only feeds the fire she wants to put out, and the closing couplet turns the complaint into a daydream of paradise. The sequence it belongs to is often called the first great English sonnet sequence.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/divi.text: Longfellow wrote this sonnet sequence while translating Dante's Divine Comedy into English, and uses it to picture the poem as a great cathedral. In the first sonnet a tired labourer sets down his burden at the door; in the second the poet looks up at the carvings, from sculpted figures to gargoyled fiends and dragons. It is a short guide to how a translator experienced the poem's size and its mix of beauty and horror.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/fall.text: A four-line epigram about a captain killed when a wall that had been undermined and battered by shot falls on him. The joke is in the last line: his tomb is a whole town, which some men would envy. Donne wrote many epigrams, and this one gets its effect in just two couplets.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/hill.text: Hilda Conkling composed her poems aloud as a child and had them written down. Here she watches a ridge of hills and decides they are on a very slow journey, like camels in a line, loaded with birches, rocks and gold leaves. The poem is short and plain, and its charm lies in how seriously the child takes the hills' effort.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/inde.text: A man who insisted that everyone stand on their own, and who would neither ask for help nor give it, is summed up in eight plain lines. The portrait builds up his pride and strength, then lets the closing sentence say how it ended for him. The poem is short enough to read twice, and on the second reading the word in the title starts to change its meaning.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/kerr.text: A two-line poem about an embrace: when the speaker is held, the summer rain dreams of oceans. The brevity forces the image to do all the work, moving from a small human gesture to a vast one. It is from Bruce Meyer's collection The Spirit Bride (2002).

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/la-n.text: A French Romantic poem in the form of a dialogue between a poet and his Muse on a May night, in which she urges him to take his lute, because spring is coming alive. He grows uneasy, hearing his heart race and seeing a veiled shape in the forest. Musset's lines are in French, and this is the first of four poems about the Muse that he wrote in the 1830s, in which the poet's pain becomes the source of his songs.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/nigh.text: A hymn text that urges work through morning, noon and sunset, because night, the end of all labour, is coming. Annie Louisa Walker's verses became a popular church hymn in the nineteenth century, and their steady rhythm and repeated first line were made to be sung. Read now, they show how a call to industry could be bound up with the thought of death.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/o-ma.text: George Eliot imagines an afterlife that is not heaven: the dead go on living in the minds they improved and in the generous acts they prompted. She wrote it as a novelist who had left orthodox Christianity, and the poem has often been read as a hymn for people without a creed. The sentences are long and stately, so it rewards reading aloud.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/ode-.text: William Collins addresses evening as a modest nymph and asks her to teach him a verse as quiet as the dusk. He fills the hush with small things: a bat's thin shriek, a beetle's hum, the first star, a sheet of lake. Unusually for an eighteenth-century ode, it does not rhyme, which gives it a slow, drifting pace.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/pray.text: A soldier on the march sets each of his aches beside the sufferings of Christ: the pack on his shoulders, his burning feet, his numb hand. Every pair of rhymed lines puts the Crucifixion in brackets, as if the prayer were murmured under his breath. Joyce Kilmer was an American soldier in the First World War and was killed in France in 1918.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/psal.text: Longfellow answers someone who says life is an empty dream with a rousing argument for action: do not be driven like cattle, live in the present, and leave something behind. The rhymed quatrains made it one of the most quoted poems of the nineteenth century, so many of its lines will feel familiar even to first-time readers. It is worth reading for how plainly it makes its case.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/reci.text: A grim eight-line joke in the shape of a recipe: scold someone and they murmur, strike them and they complain, hurt them and they whine, but thrash them properly and they will never speak again. Crosland had a name as a ferocious satirist, and the poem leaves it to the reader to decide who is being mocked, the victim or the people who believe in punishment.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/rich.text: A town watches a rich, elegant, universally admired man go down the street, and its people wish they could be in his place. Robinson holds the whole poem in the collective voice of the people on the pavement, and the last two lines turn it around with a plain, shocking fact. It is only sixteen lines, and a classic of the short poem that ends on a surprise.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/sonn.text: A woman takes out a bundle of letters from the man who loves her and goes through them one by one, remembering what each one said: that he wanted to see her as a friend, that he loved her, that he was hers. Paper that seems dead trembles in her hands. Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote the sequence this sonnet belongs to during her courtship with Robert Browning, and the poem catches the fear of whether she can dare to say it back.

rpo:rpo.library.utoronto.ca/content/what.text: A sexton speaks to the dead and tells them that their names will not outlast the churchyard. When the town grows around it, someone will build a garage or an inn there and throw the tombstone down. Vachel Lindsay ends on the moon as the sky's own tombstone, with a message of peace in the face of being forgotten.

wikisource:en.wikisource.org/wiki/Intent.text: A dialogue between Cyril and Vivian in a country-house library, in which Vivian refuses to go out and enjoy nature and argues that life imitates art far more than art imitates life. Oscar Wilde is playful and provocative, and behind the paradoxes he makes a serious case for imagination and style over plain observation. It is longer than most essays here, but it moves quickly and is full of epigrams.

wikisource:en.wikisource.org/wiki/Table-.text: Hazlitt, a painter before he became a famous essayist, describes the peace of working in front of nature: no arguments to win, no fools to endure, nobody to please. Writing, he says, means contending with the world, while painting is a friendly quarrel with nature. It is the first essay in Table-Talk and a good way into his warm, argumentative voice.

Hazlitt reads the lectures of the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds and collects passages that contradict each other, on whether excellence in art comes from hard study or from genius, and whether beauty lies in nature or in an idea in the mind. It is an essay about reading closely and arguing with an authority, by a writer who was also a painter. You need to know nothing about Reynolds, because the questions apply to any craft.

Hazlitt takes on the idea that taste and genius can be reduced to rules. His answer is that we judge by feeling and by the accumulated impression of many things, much as we walk without knowing which muscles to use. The essay is a defence of intuition in art and in daily life, argued with examples rather than theory.

wikisource:en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Es.text: Bacon argues that a little philosophy leans toward atheism but depth in philosophy leads back to religion, and that a world without a mind is harder to believe in than many old fables. The essay is very short and written in one dense flow, typical of his style. It is a good place to see how he packs an argument into a few sentences.

Bacon writes about people who look wiser than they are: those who stay solemn and mysterious, who lean on a raised eyebrow or a gesture, or who answer a hard question with a look of knowing more than they can say. He treats them as fit targets for satire and lists the tricks they use, including the raised brow Cicero noticed in Piso. It is a short essay, and a good example of his dry, compressed style.

Montaigne starts with an old rhetorician who claimed to make little things look great, and compares him to a shoemaker making a big shoe for a small foot. He judges those who dress up words as worse than women who paint their faces, because they corrupt the mind and not just the face. It is a short chapter that still applies to anyone who distrusts a good speech.

Montaigne reacts to Seneca's advice to a powerful friend to retire from ambition and luxury to a quiet, philosophical life, and asks how far one should push contempt for pleasure. He begins from the ancient view that it is time to die when life holds more ill than good. The chapter shows his habit of testing an authority against his own common sense.
